key_insight: The paper argues that autonomous agents need an "immune system" built into the agent itself, not just external security guards. By moving defense into the active reasoning loop, it aims to protect agents from runtime attacks like memory poisoning, tool misuse, and multi-agent manipulation.
problem_solved: It addresses the gap between static AI safety methods and the new risks introduced by persistent, tool-using, multi-agent systems. Existing defenses often fail once an agent is operating in the real world and can be hijacked during execution.
method: Proposes an agent-native security architecture that monitors and defends the agent during reasoning and action, rather than only before deployment.
Defines a taxonomy of threats targeting agent memory, tools, and collaboration channels.
Outlines engineering principles for integrating detection, isolation, and response mechanisms directly into agent workflows.
impact: For AI practitioners, this reframes safety as a runtime systems problem, not just a training-time alignment problem. It provides a blueprint for building more robust autonomous agents that can operate safely in open-ended environments.
visual_elements: Layered architecture diagram showing agent core, memory, tools, and immune-defense modules
Threat taxonomy chart mapping attacks to memory, tool-chain, and multi-agent surfaces
Before-vs-after flow diagram comparing external defenses to agent-native defenses
Icon set for threats and defenses, such as poison, shield, memory, tool, and network symbols
paper_title: Agent-Native Immune System: Architecture, Taxonomy, and Engineering
paper_authors: Bo Shen, Lifeng Chang, Tianyuan Wei, Yunpeng Li, Feng Shi
